sentences: On this tall scroll, a mountain, a palace and a band of trees are stacked one above another.
This is An Jung-sik's Spring Dawn at Mount Baegak, painted in 1915.
The title means 'spring dawn at Baegak'.
Let's travel slowly up and down it.
An Jung-sik was chosen as a court painter for the royal portrait of 1902.
From 1911 he trained the next generation, including Yi Sang-beom and No Su-hyeon, at the Calligraphy and Painting Academy.
Look first at the writing at the upper left.
Beside the four-character title is the inscription 'painted by Simjeon on a summer day in the eulmyo year', which tells us this is the summer version.
In 1915 he painted the same view twice, in summer and in autumn, with almost the same composition.
Some also hear in the title an echo of Spring Dawn, a famous Tang poem by Meng Haoran.
Now the peak.
Half the picture belongs to Mount Baegak, today's Bugaksan.
It is drawn larger and closer than it really is, stressing the majesty of the northern mountain guarding the palace.
Look closely at the mountain's surface.
Short, repeated strokes follow every ridge and valley, a traditional landscape technique.
Together these short strokes build up the texture and mass of Mount Baegak.
Let's move down below the mountain.
Low clouds and mist hide the lower parts of the palace.
Ink and water were allowed to blur every edge, and so the stillness of the dawn air settles over the scene.
Under the clouds, the roofs of Gyeongbokgung Palace follow one after another.
Trees and mist leave only the rooftops visible and hide everything beneath them, so the palace seems deeply asleep.
At the centre stands Gwanghwamun Gate, closed tight.
All three of its doors are shut, telling us it is very early morning.
The axis of the gate runs straight up to the mountain's peak.
Below, the haetae, guardian beasts of stone, appear half-hidden among the trees on both sides.
In this summer version we see both of them, but in the autumn version mist and trees hide the right one.
That year parts of the palace were being demolished or altered for a colonial industrial exhibition.
Yet he shows it whole and dignified, which many read as a quiet wish for independence.
Made at the request of the former royal household, the summer version passed from the Deoksugung museum to the National Museum of Korea, and became registered national heritage in 2012.
When, we might ask, will this closed gate open?
